cases.input:
Can you pull out what matters from this report? I want to know what's actually new in it.

Northfield Labs Q3 Threat Brief (fictional, example.com)

Northfield Labs tracked 412 ransomware incidents against mid-sized manufacturers in Q3, up from 301 in Q2. Median dwell time before encryption fell from 9 days to 3 days. In 58 percent of cases the initial access was a VPN appliance that had been patched but never rebooted, so the vulnerable process stayed resident in memory. Only 14 percent of victims had tested an offline restore in the previous year.

The tracked group "Pale Heron" shifted from encrypting file servers first to deleting hypervisor snapshots first, then encrypting. Analyst Priya Raman wrote: "The patch was applied. The fix was not live. Attackers noticed before defenders did." Pale Heron staged tooling on vendor-support hosts reachable at portal.example.com, reusing the vendor's own remote-management agent rather than installing new malware.

Average ransom demand was 1.9 million USD, but the median payment was 310,000 USD, 16 percent of the demand. 71 percent of negotiators reported operators accepting installment payments for the first time this quarter. Northfield recommends rebooting appliances after every firmware patch, restricting the vendor-agent's outbound access to 203.0.113.0/24, and testing restores quarterly. The report credits the open-source tool Velociraptor for triage work and a fictional insurer's claims dataset for the payment figures.
cases.expects: A plain-language one-sentence summary, then trends, statistics, exact quotes, references and recommendations drawn only from this short report, without padding to the upstream pattern's minimum counts where the material does not support them. The patched-but-unrebooted VPN finding and the shift to deleting snapshots before encrypting should surface as the genuinely new points, every number and quote reproduced exactly as written, and nothing invented beyond what the report says.

cases.input:
Run analyze_threat_report_cmds on these incident-response notes and give me the commands as a reusable checklist, with what each one is for.

Triage notes, fictional client "Calder Fabrication", case ref CF-2291:

On the suspected host (10.0.0.0/8 internal range, example corp) we pulled volatile state before isolating it: `netstat -ano` to list active connections, then `tasklist /v` to correlate PIDs to process names, then `wevtutil qe Security /q:"*[System[(EventID=4624 or EventID=4625)]]" /f:text /c:200` to pull the last 200 logon events. For the EDR side we ran a Velociraptor collection with `velociraptor.exe artifacts collect Windows.Forensics.Timeline -v` and shipped the output to our case bucket. On the firewall we queried denied outbound traffic to the staging host at 198.51.100.7 with `show log eventtype eq traffic filter dst-ip eq 198.51.100.7`. Once the host was confirmed compromised we isolated it at the switch with `shutdown vlan 40` on the access port, per our containment runbook.
cases.expects: A command-by-command breakdown in the upstream pattern's format: each command reproduced exactly as given, grouped by purpose (live-response collection, log review, EDR triage, containment), with a plain explanation of what each one does and why it was used in this investigation. Nothing added beyond what the notes describe, and no command invented that is not in the source text.

cases.input:
analyze_threat_report_trends on this. It's not really a report, just my notes mashing together two things I read this week plus a chart caption I'm not sure I'm reading right.

Note 1 (from a vendor one-pager, no byline): "Credential-stuffing attempts against retail login pages rose through the back half of the year; most tooling now rotates residential proxies per request rather than per session."

Note 2 (from a conference lightning talk, speaker not named, slides not public): the speaker claimed "half of the incidents we worked this year started with a help-desk password reset," but didn't give a sample size or time window, and I don't know if "we" means their firm's whole caseload or one team.

Chart caption I'm unsure about: "MFA bypass reports, by month, non-SMS methods in orange." The caption doesn't say what counts as a bypass report or who is reporting them, and I don't have the chart itself, just this caption.
cases.expects: Only the trends the thin material actually supports, each one flagged with how little the source backs it: the credential-stuffing proxy-rotation point can be stated plainly since the note commits to it, but the help-desk-reset claim should be marked as a single unsourced assertion with no sample size, and the MFA-bypass caption should be flagged as too ambiguous (no definition of 'bypass report', no chart data) to state as a trend rather than invented or stated as fact. Padding out to any minimum trend count with generic industry trends not present in this material would be the wrong answer.
